new_statements.translation: TONES. For the moment, in this domain, we will confine ourselves to pointing out that we have noted three distinct levels: high, mid and low, and that they do not seem to combine with a stress (intensity) accent. But we will need to complete our survey before we can say whether the three levels noted are phonological or phonetic, given the modifications that occur and that are tied to morpho-syntactic rules. There are also, on long vowels, melodic realisations of generally rising register.

new_statements.rule_in_words: Kyanga (Tyanga) is a three-level tone language (H, M, L); the field notes report no stress/intensity accent co-occurring with the tones, i.e. no word stress was observed -- stated tentatively, pending fuller analysis. Jones 2010 independently confirms three level lexical tones on every syllable and says nothing about stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None regarding stress. Author hedges that the whole tonal analysis is provisional ('ne semblent pas', 'pour le moment'); tones are altered by morpho-syntactic conditioning (verb tense marked by tone, pp. 80-81), long vowels carry rising contours; base tones of most lexemes not yet established so tones are mostly left unmarked (p. 85).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phonetic inventory based on c. 1000 elicited words per lect (Kasati for Tyanga, Sakaci for Shanga), some in isolation, most in short sentences; the single phonetic table and remarks are stated to hold for both Tyanga and Shanga.
new_statements.identity_note: Platiel 1982 describes 'le tyanga' as spoken at Kasati (Kasaci), Kebbi State, Nigeria -- the village Jones 2010 names as having 'the purest form of Kyanga' -- i.e. kyen1242 itself; her phonetic section (pp. 85-91, incl. the tone/accent statement) is explicitly given as one table valid for both Tyanga and Shanga (shan1282, data from Sakaci), so the same sentence also covers Shanga. Jones 2010 covers Kyanga (Kasati, Tungan Bage, Tondi, Sarafu, Tungan Noma) and Shanga separately.

sources.citation: Jones, Ross McCallum. 2010. Preliminary report on the Kyanga and Shanga. Ms., July 2010, 20 pp. (formerly at mandelang.kunstkamera.ru/files/mandelang/; Wayback 2018 capture).
sources.note: Silent on stress. Sec. 7.0 Phonology, 'Tone' p. 11: 'Every syllable in the Kyanga language has a tone... There are 3 level tones - high (H), mid (M) and (L)'; polysyllabic nouns tend to be all mid; many words have lost tone relative to Boko/Busa; acute/grave accents are orthographic tone marks. Shanga sec. 5.0 p. 19: phonology 'similar to Kyanga'.
